title: The rainmakers, 1946
teaches: How dry ice and silver iodide make a supercooled cloud snow, how much is enough, which clouds seeding can and can’t work on, and how to tell a real effect from a lucky winter

blocks.title: The big ideas of this lesson
points: Most clouds between 0 °C and −20 °C are **supercooled**: liquid water below freezing, waiting for something to start ice. Once there is ice, it grows at the droplets’ expense and falls as snow. What such a cloud lacks is not water but ice.
**Dry ice** (−78 °C) makes ice by sheer cold, in any cloud colder than 0 °C. **Silver iodide** makes ice by looking like it, in clouds colder than about −5 °C.
Seeding a layer with the right amount of ice snows a hole in it. Too little gives a few flurries; too much gives crystals too small to fall: **overseeding**.
Seeding cannot make a cloud, or water. It works in a window, about −5 to −25 °C. It clears supercooled fog every time, and adds a little snow to winter clouds over mountains.
Storms vary so much by themselves that only a fair trial, with the storms to seed picked by chance, over many winters, can show whether seeding did anything.

blocks.text: Lesson 7 left a puzzle unfinished. Most clouds between 0 °C and −20 °C are made of liquid droplets, below freezing but not frozen: **supercooled**. A droplet freezes only when something gives its molecules a template to line up on. Every litre of air carries millions of specks of dust, salt and smoke, but hardly any of them are shaped right to be that template.

Count them in a litre of cloud at −10 °C. There are about a hundred thousand droplets, and perhaps one ice-starting speck in every 250 litres. Colder, the specks that work grow more common, about tenfold for every 4 °C, but even at −15 °C there is only one in a dozen litres. A cloud like that can sit for hours, full of water that would fall as snow if only it had some ice.

blocks.caption: How rare ice-starting specks are, against the droplets in a litre of cloud.

blocks.text: Because once there is ice, Lesson 7’s machinery takes over: vapour leaves the droplets and freezes straight onto the crystals, which grow heavy enough to fall in a quarter of an hour, as snow that may melt into rain lower down. So in a supercooled cloud, the rain is held back not by a shortage of water but by a shortage of ice. That is the whole idea behind cloud seeding: give the cloud the ice it is missing.

In 1946, at the General Electric laboratory in Schenectady, New York, Vincent Schaefer was working with the chemist Irving Langmuir on how ice forms on aeroplanes: supercooled droplets that hit a wing freeze onto it, just like rime on a fence. To study them, Schaefer made clouds of his own.

He used an ordinary chest freezer, lined it with black velvet, and breathed into it. His breath made a small cloud of droplets that stayed supercooled at −10 to −20 °C. A lamp shining across the box lit up any ice crystal as a tiny glint against the black. Schaefer dropped in talc, salt, sulphur, soil and dozens of other dusts, hoping to find one that would start ice. Hardly anything did.

One hot day in July 1946, the freezer was struggling to stay cold, and Schaefer dropped in a lump of dry ice to cool it down. At once the light beam filled with millions of glittering crystals, and the whole cloud turned to ice and settled to the floor of the box as snow.

blocks.caption: A freezer full of breath-cloud, lit from the side, as in Schaefer’s laboratory. Pick the temperature, then drop something in.
blocks.task: Make it snow in the box.

blocks.text: Try each thing at a few temperatures. Above 0 °C, nothing works, not even dry ice: there is no supercooled water, and any crystals it makes melt as soon as they leave its trail. Below 0 °C, a pinch of dust (far more specks than clean air holds) starts a few crystals only when the box is very cold, too few to take the cloud’s water. Silver iodide smoke does nothing until about −5 °C and then fills the box. Dry ice works at every temperature below freezing.

Dry ice is frozen carbon dioxide, at −78 °C. It is not a template at all; it works by cold alone. A falling pellet chills a thin trail of air behind it below −40 °C, and there, as Lesson 7 showed, droplets freeze by themselves, with no speck needed. Vapour in the trail turns straight into tiny crystals too, by deposition.[^deposition]

blocks.caption: Why a pellet of dry ice makes so much ice.

blocks.text: Each gram of dry ice leaves hundreds of billions of crystals behind it. They drift out of the trail into the surrounding cloud, which can be at any temperature below freezing, and grow there at the droplets’ expense.

Dry ice has a drawback: it has to be carried up in an aeroplane and dropped into the cloud, or onto its top, and a pellet is used up in a fall of a kilometre or two. It works only where it is put, and only in cloud colder than 0 °C.

On 13 November 1946, Schaefer flew over Mount Greylock in western Massachusetts with a few pounds of crushed dry ice and dropped it along a line across the top of a supercooled cloud layer. Within five minutes the cloud below his path had turned to snow, which streamed out of its base in long trails. The air beneath was dry, and the snow evaporated before it reached the ground. But for the first time, someone had made a cloud snow on purpose.

Bernard Vonnegut, a chemist in the same laboratory[^vonnegut], took a different approach. If the rare natural specks work because their atoms are arranged like ice, why not find a substance whose crystals are arranged like ice and make a great deal of it?

He searched tables of crystal shapes and found **silver iodide**. Its crystals are six-sided, like ice, and its atoms sit just 1.5 percent further apart than the molecules in ice: 0.459 against 0.452 nanometres, where a nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre. A supercooled droplet that touches a speck of silver iodide finds a template almost as good as ice itself. In November 1946, its smoke filled the cold box with crystals.

Silver iodide has two great advantages over dry ice. A little goes a very long way: a single gram, burned into smoke, makes about a million billion specks, ten thousand times as many crystals as a gram of dry ice. And it does not have to be dropped from above: smoke from burners on the ground can be carried up into clouds over the mountains by the wind.

blocks.caption: Getting the ice into the cloud: smoke from a burner on the ground, carried up the slopes by the wind, or pellets from an aeroplane.

blocks.text: Its drawback is that the match with ice is close but not perfect. A droplet on a perfect template would freeze just below 0 °C; on silver iodide it needs to be chilled five degrees or so more before its molecules will line up on the slightly wrong spacing. So silver iodide needs the cloud to be colder than about −5 °C, works better and better as it gets colder, and is at its best below −10 °C. In a cloud at −3 °C, dry ice works and silver iodide does not.

parts.title: Opening a hole in the sky

blocks.text: What happens when a whole layer of supercooled cloud is seeded? The crystals share out the layer’s water between them, and how much each one gets decides everything. Seeders measured dose by the pound: a rule of thumb from the first flights was about a pound of dry ice for every mile flown, which makes about fifty crystals in every litre of the layer below.

With very few crystals, each one has plenty of water to itself and grows big, but there are too few of them to empty the layer: a few flurries fall, and the cloud carries on. With between about five and three thousand crystals in each litre, the water is taken quickly, the crystals grow big enough to fall, and the layer snows itself out, leaving a hole.

With far too many crystals, more than about three thousand in each litre, the water is shared out so thinly that every crystal stays tiny, too small to fall. The cloud turns from droplets to ice and simply hangs there as a silky veil. That is **overseeding**, and a pilot who thinks more is always better will get it.

blocks.caption: A supercooled layer, seeded from an aeroplane flying above it. The scales below show how many crystals each litre gets, and how big each grows. The temperature slider shows the one thing dry ice can’t do: seed a layer warmer than 0 °C.
blocks.task: Seed the layer just enough to snow a hole in it.

blocks.text: In the figure, the snow falls clear to the ground. In real air it often doesn’t: if the air under the cloud is dry, the snow evaporates on its way down, as Schaefer’s did over Mount Greylock. For seeding to put anything on the ground, the cloud must be deep enough to grow big flakes, and the air under it moist enough to let them through.
Seeding at its best is impressive: a cloud that turns to snow minutes after a pass with dry ice. Its limits matter just as much to anyone deciding whether to pay for it.
The first limit is the simplest. Seeding does not make clouds, and it does not make water. It only gives ice to a cloud that already holds supercooled water. No cloud, nothing to seed.

In a drought, the sky is usually clear for a reason. A high sits over the region and its air sinks, warming and drying as it is squeezed, as in Lesson 2. To make a cloud, air has to be lifted and cooled to its dew point, as in Lesson 1, and no amount of dry ice can lift the air over a whole county.

And a cloud holds very little water at any moment, about 0.2 mm’s worth, as Lesson 2 showed; a storm rains for hours only because it keeps lifting new moist air. So seeding can only help a cloud let go of more of the water passing through it while it is there.

The third limit is temperature. Seeding needs supercooled water, so it does nothing for a cloud warmer than 0 °C. Between 0 and −5 °C, only dry ice works, because silver iodide, a near but imperfect match for ice, needs the droplets chilled a few degrees more. Between about −5 and −25 °C, dry ice and silver iodide both work, and this is where seeding has the most to offer.

Colder than that, nature catches up. Natural ice-starting specks grow about tenfold more common for every 4 °C colder (the first figure of this lesson drew them), so somewhere around −25 °C there are enough of them to freeze the cloud without help; the change is gradual, not a sharp line. Below −38 °C droplets freeze by themselves, and the cloud is all ice, like cirrus. Adding ice to a cloud that already has plenty does nothing useful.

blocks.caption: Which clouds seeding can help, by temperature. On the left, how high each temperature is: in summer, 0 °C is about 3 km up; in winter it can be at the ground.

blocks.text: How cold a cloud is depends on the season as much as on its height. Summer cumulus over the basin is usually warmer than 0 °C all the way through, so there is nothing to seed. By the time a summer heap grows far above the freezing level, it is a thunderstorm already full of its own ice. Seeding it can make it grow a little faster (freezing releases heat, like condensation in Lesson 5) or do nothing at all; experiments have never settled which.

The best candidates are the cold clouds of winter, when even low cloud is below freezing: the supercooled fog and stratus that pools in the basin under an inversion, and the clouds that winter storms pile up over the mountains.

**Supercooled fog** is seeding’s one sure success. Dry ice dropped from an aeroplane fills a fog bank with crystals; so does propane gas sprayed from a nozzle on the ground, which expands as it leaves the nozzle and, like rising air in Lesson 1, chills itself and the air around it below −40 °C. The crystals grow, fall as a light snow, and open a clear hole over a runway for an hour or so. It works every time, but only in supercooled fog; fog warmer than 0 °C does not respond at all.

blocks.caption: Clearing supercooled fog over a runway.

blocks.text: **Winter clouds over mountains** are the other good case. Moist air forced up the western slopes makes supercooled cloud, and much of it crosses the crest before its water has turned to snow, then evaporates down the far side, as in the rain shadow of Lesson 7. That is where the mountain seeding of the figure above comes in.

Silver iodide from burners on the ground, or from aircraft, can turn some of that passing water into snow on the slopes. Careful experiments have measured gains from a few percent up to perhaps fifteen percent, in the right storms: cloud deep enough to grow big flakes, and air under it moist enough that the snow reaches the ground instead of evaporating on the way down. For dry country downstream, that matters: mountain snow is the river water of summer.

**Hailstorms and hurricanes** have been seeded too, in the hope of making many small hailstones instead of a few large ones, or of weakening a hurricane’s winds. Neither has ever been clearly shown to work. Storms that big have so much energy and so much natural ice that a seeder’s contribution is lost in them.
The hardest question in cloud seeding is whether it did anything. A seeder seeds a cloud, and it snows. Would it have snowed anyway?

Storms vary enormously by themselves. One winter storm over the mountains may drop three times the snow of the next for reasons that have nothing to do with seeding. An effect of ten or fifteen percent is a whisper next to that noise.

The only fair test is the one doctors use for a new medicine. Decide which storms to seed by chance, with a coin toss, before anyone knows how each will turn out.[^trial] Then compare many seeded storms with many that were not. Luck evens out only when there are a great many storms on each side. A second check is to compare the seeded area with a **control** area nearby that was not seeded but gets the same storms: weather that hits both cancels out, and what is left is more likely to be the seeding.

blocks.caption: A seeding trial over the mountains, where seeding truly adds 15 percent. Each dot is one storm’s snow, measured as water; the scale stretches the small storms out, so equal steps along it mean equal multiples. Below: how many times the snow the seeded storms got, with the range luck alone allows.
blocks.task: Run winters until the difference stands out from luck.

blocks.text: Notice two things in the figure. Press “New winters” at one or two winters: seeding can look as if it doubled the snow, or as if it made things worse. That is luck, not seeding. And when the seeder picks the storms, the numbers look wonderful and mean almost nothing, because a good forecaster picks the storms that were going to snow anyway: the dashed line shows what those same storms would have brought unseeded.

Rainmakers made exactly that mistake, or took advantage of it, long before dry ice. Charles Hatfield, the most famous, was hired by San Diego in 1915 to fill a reservoir; he set up his towers of secret chemicals, and the rains came, and flooded the valley.[^hatfield] He and others like him worked when rain looked likely, and took the credit when it came.

Radar at last let seeders watch their snow being made. In 2017, in the mountains of Idaho, a research team flew an aeroplane back and forth across the wind, releasing silver iodide along straight lines upwind of their radars, on days when the cloud was supercooled and making little snow by itself. Lines of snow appeared on the radar screens, each one drifting downwind and spreading as it went, in the same pattern as the aeroplane’s path. It was the first time anyone had followed seeded snow from the seeding to the ground. On many other days, though, the lines could not be picked out from the natural snow at all, so a fair test over many storms is still the only way to say what seeding adds over a whole winter.

blocks.caption: Seeded snow on radar, seen from above, as in the Idaho experiment: three passes of the aeroplane, three lines of snow drifting downwind.

blocks.text: So when someone asks a seeder to make it rain, the honest answer has a few parts. Nobody can make clouds. Sometimes you can help a supercooled cloud let go of water it would otherwise have carried away. In the right clouds, expect a small gain; in the wrong ones, nothing. And be ready to show how you know.

Every lesson in this workbook comes into that answer: what a cloud is made of, how air is lifted to make one, which floor it lives on and how cold it is there, how ice makes rain, and what kind of storm it belongs to.

blocks.title: Before you seed, ask
points: Is there a cloud? Seeding cannot make one.
Is it supercooled, between about −5 and −25 °C? From 0 to −5 °C only dry ice works; above 0 °C nothing does; colder than −25 °C, it has its own ice.
Is it deep enough, and the air below it moist enough, for snow to reach the ground?
How much will you use? Too much overseeds: crystals too small to fall.
How will you know it worked? Seed by chance, compare with storms left alone, and count many winters.

blocks.text: Seeding needs supercooled cloud, so start with what kind of cloud it is and which floor it lives on. Remember that in winter even a low cloud can be supercooled. First call the floor of each cloud in the photos. Then answer what seeding can and can’t do for each sky.

blocks.caption: Real photos. Which floor is each cloud on?
A sky to seed, or not? What would seeding do?

items.question: On a hot July afternoon, small cumulus have bases at 1.5 km and tops at 2.5 km. The freezing level is 4 km up. Will dropping dry ice into them make rain?
options: Yes: dry ice is cold enough to make rain from any cloud at all
No: they are warmer than 0 °C all through, with nothing to freeze
Yes, but only silver iodide, because the cloud is too warm for dry ice
items.why: Seeding gives ice to supercooled water. These clouds never reach the freezing level, so their droplets are ordinary warm water; dry ice chills a trail for a moment, and the cloud carries on.

items.question: A pilot dumped his whole load into a supercooled layer: a hundred pounds a mile. The layer turned white and silky, but not a flake fell. Why?
options: The dry ice melted away before it ever reached the cloud
The cloud was too warm for dry ice to start any ice
Overseeding: the crystals shared the water and stayed too small
items.why: The crystals share out the cloud’s water. With thousands in every litre, each gets only a speck and never grows heavy enough to fall. About a pound a mile is enough to snow a hole.

items.question: A grey deck has sat over the county for three days at about −8 °C, and there’s rime on every fence post. I’ve got two hundred pounds of dry ice in the duster. Will it do anything?
options: Yes: the rime says it’s supercooled. Spread it thin, a pound a mile
No: dry ice only works on summer clouds, high above the freezing level
No: at −8 °C the cloud is too cold to turn into snow at all
items.why: Rime is supercooled droplets freezing on contact, so the deck is liquid below freezing: just what seeding works on. Spread it thin: about a pound a mile, not the whole load.

items.question: I watched the snow come streaming out of the cloud where the duster went over, but none of it reached my roof. Did the seeding fail?
options: Yes: if no snow reached the ground, the seeding did nothing
No: the cloud snowed, but the dry air below took it back
The snow all blew east on the wind and landed in Idaho
items.why: Trails of snow that hang from a cloud and vanish on the way down are virga. The seeding worked on the cloud; the dry air beneath took the snow back, just as it did over Mount Greylock in 1946.

items.question: No rain in six weeks, a few flat little heaps at noon that never grow, and the barometer high and steady. A man from California wants two thousand dollars to make it rain. Should the Grange hire him?
options: Yes: seeding works on any cloud, however small it is
Yes, but only if he seeds the heaps at night, when they’re cold
No: there is no supercooled cloud here for him to seed
items.why: Under a high, sinking air keeps the heaps small, flat and warm. Seeding cannot lift air or make cloud; it can only give ice to supercooled water, and there is none here.

items.question: The doctor from Spokane can’t land for the fog. It’s −7 °C and there’s rime on everything. Can anything be done?
options: No: fog can never be cleared, only waited out
Wait for a thunderstorm to come and blow it away
Yes: seed the fog over the runway with dry ice
items.why: Rime means the fog is supercooled. Dry ice fills it with crystals that grow and fall as a light snow, clearing a hole over the runway long enough to land.

items.question: A seeder picked five storms to seed last winter, and they snowed 40 percent more than the average storm. Does that prove seeding works?
options: No: he picked them himself, and five storms are far too few
Yes: 40 percent is far too big a difference to be luck
Yes, as long as all five of the storms were in winter
items.why: A seeder with a good eye picks the storms that were going to snow anyway, and five storms vary far more than seeding could. Only storms picked by chance, over many winters, can show a real effect.

learned: A supercooled cloud can stay liquid for hours below 0 °C, because ice-starting specks are rare; once ice appears, it grows at the droplets’ expense and falls as snow, so what holds back the snow is a shortage of ice, not of water.

Dry ice (−78 °C) chills its trail below −40 °C and works in any cloud colder than 0 °C; silver iodide’s crystals match ice to within 1.5 percent and start ice below about −5 °C, and its smoke can be sent up from the ground.
A seeded layer with tens to hundreds of crystals per litre snows out, leaving a hole; too few give flurries, and too many (overseeding) stay too small to fall.

Seeding cannot make clouds or water. It works in a window, roughly −5 to −25 °C; it reliably clears supercooled fog and adds perhaps up to fifteen percent to winter mountain snow, and has never been clearly shown to tame hailstorms or hurricanes.
Only a fair trial, with storms to seed picked by chance and compared over many winters and with an unseeded control area, can show whether seeding did anything.

supercooled.title: Clouds waiting for ice
supercooled.text: Most clouds between 0 °C and −20 °C are supercooled liquid, because ice-starting specks are so rare: about one in every few hundred litres at −10 °C, against a hundred thousand droplets in each litre. Once ice appears, it grows at the droplets’ expense and falls as snow, so a supercooled cloud is short of ice, not of water. That shortage is what cloud seeding fills.

dry-ice.title: Dry ice
dry-ice.text: Frozen carbon dioxide at −78 °C. A falling pellet chills its trail below −40 °C, where droplets and vapour freeze without any speck, leaving hundreds of billions of crystals per gram. It works in any cloud colder than 0 °C but must be dropped from an aeroplane. Vincent Schaefer found it in his cold box at General Electric in July 1946 and first seeded a cloud with it over Mount Greylock, Massachusetts, on 13 November 1946.

silver-iodide.title: Silver iodide
silver-iodide.text: A six-sided crystal whose atoms sit only 1.5 percent further apart than the molecules of ice, so supercooled droplets freeze on it as if it were ice. It starts working below about −5 °C, and best below −10 °C. One gram burned into smoke makes about a million billion specks, which burners on the ground can send up into mountain clouds. Bernard Vonnegut found it in November 1946.

overseeding.title: Seeding a layer
overseeding.text: Seeded crystals share out a cloud’s water. A few per litre grow big but leave the layer as it was; tens to hundreds per litre snow it out, leaving a hole; thousands per litre each get so little water that they stay too small to fall, and the layer turns into a lingering veil of ice. An early rule of thumb was a pound of dry ice per mile flown.

seeding-window.title: The seeding window
seeding-window.text: Seeding needs supercooled water and a shortage of natural ice. Above 0 °C there is nothing to freeze; from 0 to −5 °C only dry ice works; from about −5 to −25 °C dry ice and silver iodide both work; colder, natural specks make enough ice already, and below −38 °C clouds are all ice.

seeding-works.title: Where seeding works
seeding-works.text: It clears supercooled fog every time, opening a hole over a runway for an hour or so. Over mountains in winter, silver iodide can turn some of the supercooled cloud that would have crossed the crest into snow on the slopes: careful experiments find a few percent to perhaps fifteen percent more, in the right storms. For hail and hurricanes, no clear effect has ever been shown.

fair-trial.title: A fair trial
fair-trial.text: Storms vary so much by themselves that one winter, or a seeder’s own pick of storms, proves nothing. Pick the storms to seed by chance, compare many seeded storms with many left alone, over many winters, and compare the seeded area with an unseeded control area nearby. A real effect of ten or fifteen percent takes hundreds of storms to see.

deposition.title: Deposition and sublimation
deposition.text: **Deposition** is vapour turning straight into ice without passing through liquid, as frost grows on a cold window. The reverse, ice turning straight into vapour, is **sublimation**: it is how snow slowly vanishes on a cold, dry, sunny day without ever melting, and how a lump of dry ice shrinks away to nothing.

vonnegut.title: Ice-nine
vonnegut.text: Bernard’s younger brother Kurt worked in General Electric’s publicity office at the time and heard the laboratory’s stories. In his novel *Cat’s Cradle* (1963) he imagined *ice-nine*, a form of ice that is such a perfect template that one crystal freezes every drop of water it touches, and with it the world’s oceans. Silver iodide is the gentle, real version.

trial.title: Randomized trial
trial.text: Choosing by chance makes it a **randomized trial**, and leaving storms or an area unseeded gives it a **control**. A result called *statistically significant* is one that luck alone would rarely produce, by convention less than one time in twenty. It does not mean the effect is large; only that it is probably real.

hatfield.title: Who pays for a flood?
hatfield.text: Hatfield had been promised $10,000 to fill the Morena reservoir. It filled, but the January 1916 floods also burst a dam downstream, swept away bridges and killed some twenty people. The city council refused to pay, calling the rain an act of God; if Hatfield claimed it, he could answer for the damage too. He sued, and never got the money.
